old: Its ancestor described someone who hurls something across a space — in this case, an accusation.
The Greek original literally meant 'to throw across,' and came to mean 'slanderer.'
It shares a Latin root with diablo and diabolus, words for the same fallen figure.
clues: This supernatural figure started out as a courtroom insult: its ancient Greek source meant a false accuser or slanderer, someone throwing accusations at you.
The chief spirit of evil, often pictured with horns, tail and pitchfork. It's the common noun, not the name Satan, though translators used it for that Hebrew title.
People say 'speak of the ___' when someone arrives right on cue, and a mischievous child is a little one. Spanish has the cousin word diablo.
